questions.q: What does 'upstream' mean relative to a given dataset?
options: Everything that feeds it — the sources and transformations before it
Everything that consumes it — the reports built on top of it
Only the very first source system in the entire organization
Any dataset stored in the same database
questions.explain: Upstream is everything that feeds the dataset in question — its sources and the transformations data passed through to arrive there.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say 'upstream' and 'downstream' are relative terms, not absolute labels?
options: Because a dataset can be downstream of one thing and upstream of another at the same time, depending on your reference point
Because the terms only apply to cloud data warehouses
Because every dataset is always both a source and a report simultaneously
Because lineage direction changes randomly between tool vendors
questions.explain: A staging table is downstream of its source and upstream of the fact table built from it at the same time — the labels only make sense once you fix which dataset you're starting from.

questions.q: In the chain SourceTable -> StagingView -> FactTable -> Report, what does reading right to left represent?
options: Walking upstream, to see what feeds the Report
Walking downstream, to see what the SourceTable produces
Deleting each dataset in reverse order
Nothing — lineage chains can only be read left to right
questions.explain: Reading right to left walks the arrows backward — upstream — which is exactly what you do to find what feeds a given dataset.

questions.q: Per this lesson, which question requires walking the dependency graph downstream?
options: A change is proposed upstream — what breaks?
A number in a report looks wrong — where did the error start?
What file format does the source system export?
Who owns the source system?
questions.explain: Lessons 14-15's impact analysis walks downstream from a proposed change to find what it would break; walking upstream (Lesson 16) is for root-cause questions instead.

questions.q: Why is lineage usually drawn as a graph rather than a single straight-line chain?
options: Because a dataset typically has multiple upstream dependencies and multiple downstream dependents at once, not just one path
Because graphs are required by most regulatory frameworks
Because a straight-line chain cannot be stored in a database
Because every dataset in an organization connects to every other dataset
questions.explain: Real systems branch: a FactTable often has several upstream StagingViews feeding it, and one StagingView can feed several downstream FactTables and Reports — a graph captures that, a single chain doesn't.
